extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political science; scholars and general readers interested in comparative politics and U.S. elections
extracted.subtask_description: Analytical exposition of how U.S. presidential nominations, conventions, and campaigns operate — why issues or personalities dominate, how conventions function, and what effects these have on public life and political education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Issue-framing by parties
rubrics_metrics.description: "The aim of each party is to force on its antagonist certain issues which the antagonist rarely accepts..." — parties commonly select and press issues that the other side does not directly accept or traverse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate campaigns by whether the issues presented are genuine points of contention between parties or manufactured topics intended to put the opponent on the defensive. Note examples in text (e.g., Protection vs Free Trade) where issue-framing determined discourse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tangible economic issues produce educative campaigns
rubrics_metrics.description: Campaigns directed to tangible economic issues (e.g., the Free Silver issue of 1896) are described as "splendidly stimulating and educative."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the educational value of a campaign by the extent it focuses on concrete economic doctrines and arguments rather than declamatory rhetoric. The text treats 1896 (and 1904/1908 to some degree) as positive examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Platform sincerity and convergence
rubrics_metrics.description: Both parties often profess similar objects (e.g., both declared against monopolists and professed civil service reform) though neither may sincerely pursue them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge party platforms for sincerity and distinctiveness. If platforms converge in rhetoric but differ little in practice, the campaign's informative value and choice clarity are reduced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Party loyalty vs issue-based voting
rubrics_metrics.description: "The American, like the Englishman, usually votes with his party, right or wrong, and when there is little distinction of view between the parties it becomes all the easier to stick to your old friends."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure the degree to which voters are influenced by partisan loyalty versus substantive issue differences; low inter-party distinction typically increases straight-party voting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal issues substitute when controversy is languid
rubrics_metrics.description: "When political controversy is languid, personal issues come to the front... No questions raise so much warmth ... as questions affecting the character and conduct of individual men."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate campaigns for whether personal attacks replace substantive debate. Consider effects on decorum, the intensity of rhetoric, and the public's ability to evaluate evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Categories of personal censures (war record, integrity, private life)
rubrics_metrics.description: Personal attacks fall into three classes: the candidate's 'war record,' charges impeaching personal integrity, and charges about private life (especially relations with women).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing campaign negatives, classify attacks by these categories and consider historical credibility, frequency, and public sensitivity (text notes war record and private-life charges have differing historical impacts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of extravagant abuse on public confidence
rubrics_metrics.description: "Extravagant abuse produces a reaction, and makes the honest supporters of a candidate defend even his questionable acts... the confidence of the country in the honour of its public men was lowered."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the systemic effect of pervasive invective: does universal denunciation lead voters to discount all charges and reduce overall trust in public officials?

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative importance of personal qualities in presidential systems
rubrics_metrics.description: "The personal qualities of a President generally make more difference to the United States than the personal qualities of a prime minister do to Britain."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for institutional differences when evaluatingCandidates: in presidential systems personal attributes may legitimately weigh heavier in voter choice and governance outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Programme-based vs personality-based contests (educational value)
rubrics_metrics.description: British elections are characterized as "primarily one of programmes and not of persons," offering more appeal to reason and instruction; American contests often emphasize persons and oratory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate a campaign's instructiveness by whether debate centers on programmes and policies (higher instructional value) versus personalities and rhetoric (lower instructional value). Use cross-national comparisons where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nominating convention as institutional response
rubrics_metrics.description: The national nominating convention is described as "the natural and legitimate outgrowth" of constitutional features (restricted Congress functions and popular sovereignty) intended to choose a candidate the whole party respects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing nomination methods, consider representativeness and constitutional logic: conventions were created to give the people (via delegates) the right to nominate a nationally recognized candidate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conventions distract from declaring party tenets
rubrics_metrics.description: "The duty of declaring [party tenets] is commonly overshadowed by the other duty of choosing the candidate... delegates are chosen ... rather as the partisans of this or that aspirant than as persons of political ability or moral weight."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge conventions on whether they effectively formulate party programmes or whether candidate selection and factionalism crowd out substantive platform-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliberative incapacity of very large conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: National conventions are "monster public meetings" with thousands of spectators; such meetings "are capable neither of discussing political questions and settling a political programme, nor of deliberately weighing the merits of rival aspirants."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the deliberative quality of any large assembly by its size, procedural control (small committee prepares platform), and tendency to follow a few leaders rather than reasoned debate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convention leadership types (intriguer and declaimer)
rubrics_metrics.description: Conventions tend to produce two sorts of leaders — 'the intriguer' who manipulates delegates and 'the declaimer' or orator who browbeats antagonists; wisdom and knowledge are in little demand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze who succeeds in convention settings: skill in manipulation or oratorical presence often trumps statesmanship or expertise; consider how that shapes candidate selection and party quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Size and simultaneity amplify excitability and tension
rubrics_metrics.description: Very large numbers plus important issues (and the simultaneity of national polling) create intense excitement: conventions and national elections "quickens the pulse" and produce a tension not found in smaller or staggered contests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the emotional/performative dimension of campaigns by measuring size (delegates, spectators, electorate) and the simultaneity of national decision-making; high values correlate with spectacle and mass enthusiasm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Length and intensity of presidential contests are historical survivals
rubrics_metrics.description: The length of the presidential contest is described as "a survival" from times of slow communication; modern railways/telegraphs could shorten campaigns, but tradition, patronage, and rarity of the office sustain intensity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When recommending or assessing campaign duration, consider historical inertia versus present communications capacity, and institutional incentives (patronage, infrequency) that maintain long, intense contests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural appetite for excitement and large-scale spectacles
rubrics_metrics.description: "The Americans like excitement... They surrender themselves to the enjoyment of this pleasure... The American imagination is peculiarly sensitive to the impression of great size. 'A big thing' is their habitual phrase of admiration."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for cultural factors (taste for spectacle, competition, and scale) when explaining campaign tactics (parades, bands, badges) and voter responsiveness to mass demonstrations.
